study.title: Isaiah 23 The judgment on Tyre and the sanctification of his wealth
study.overview: Isaiah 23 announces the fall of Tyre, a maritime city and center of trade, and shows that its ruin is not mere economic accident, but act of the LORD of hosts. The chapter exposes the vanity of commercial pride, the instability of the wealth of nations and, at the same time, the possibility of God redirecting to the gains of a city previously marked by unclean trade for its service. The prophecy goes from the lament through destruction to the proclamation of temporary restoration and, finally, to the consecration of trade to the LORD.

outline.title: I fight for the fall of the shopping center
outline.explanation: The chapter begins with the outcry of the ships of Tarshish and the residents of the coast in front of the ruin of Tyre. The city appears as an ancient and influential commercial warehouse, supported by maritime routes and trade with Sidon. The image of silence and shame shows that the source of economic security has collapsed.

outline.title: The regional impact and theological cause of judgment
outline.explanation: The news of the fall hits Egypt and shakes other peoples linked to maritime trade. The text then interrupts the lament to affirm clearly who decreed the event: the LORD of hosts, who humiliates the pride of Tyre and slaughters the illustrious of the earth.

outline.title: Destruction of fortresses and announcement of wide ruin
outline.explanation: The language expands to include Tarshish, Canaan and the land of the Chaldeans, showing that judgment reaches strongholds and kingdoms. Verse 13 is difficult, but the general sense, by the given notes, is that the Chaldeans also appear as an example of a people whose fortress has been ruined, strengthening God's sovereignty over empires.

outline.title: Seventy years, return and consecration of earnings
outline.explanation: The desolation of Tyre is not presented as definitive: after seventy years, the city returns to commercial activity. However, the culmination is surprising: their profits cease to serve pride and become consecrated to the Lord, for the benefit of those who dwell before him, with food and clothing of good quality.

study.context: The notes indicate Tyre as an important port city and center of trade of the old known world, with ancient relations with Israel in the days of David and Solomon. Their prosperity depended on the sea and wide commercial networks, including Sidon, Egypt and Tarshish. The notes also associate the initial ruin with the Babylonian attack under Nebuchadnezzar and observe that the theme of the riches of nations turning to God reappears in Isaiah 60 and 61. The chapter therefore speaks from a historical reality of international trade, but interprets these facts as an act of divine government.
study.theology: The chapter teaches that economic prosperity is not a sign of human autonomy, but something subject to God's decree. Tyre is judged not only for its material fall, but by pride linked to its beauty and reputation. The LORD of hosts appears as he that overthrowth strongholds, shames pride, and reveals the fragility of all earthly glory. At the same time, the text shows an amazing grace: God can restore and even redirect goods acquired in an unclean way to his service. Thus, the chapter confronts the idolatry of wealth and points to God's sovereignty over commerce, kingdoms and history, including the final use of resources.

scholarViews.insight: The note highlights that although Tyre's gains came from unfair trade, these profits would be delivered to the Lord and used for worthy livelihood of his servants rather than being wasted.
Matthew Henry emphasizes that Tyre was a maritime city whose honor, wealth and activity depended on his shipping; therefore, the fall of ships represents his complete ruin.

Adam Clarke understands that the prophecy announces the destruction of Tyre by Nebuchadnezzar long before its fulfillment, when the city was still in great prosperity, showing the predictive force of the text.

questions: In what ways can confidence in wealth, economic stability or prestige become a form of pride before God?
What does it mean in practice what resources obtained in a sinful or doubtful way can be redirected to the service of the Lord?
How does this chapter help to see economic and political crises not only as human events, but also as times when God reveals his sovereignty?
study.practice: This chapter calls the reader to review his relationship with money, security and reputation. Instead of treating prosperity as a guarantee of personal value, the biblical answer is humility and dependence on the Lord. In practice, this means using goods with generosity, rejecting financial pride, supporting God's work with honestly obtained resources and remembering that every economic structure is provisional. It is also appropriate to assess whether our work serves only self-ged or whether it can be placed in a holy way at the service of the good of God's neighbor and glory.
study.uncertainty: Verse 13 is obscure in the text itself and, in the given notes, receives different explanations; therefore, the interpretation was maintained at a general level, without stating details beyond what the sources support. Nor is it possible, based only on the given notes, to safely determine all the later historical elements linked to the final fulfillment of the prophecy.
